newsitem.title: USA: U.S. FERC backs jurisdiction split on Calif. power.
newsitem.headline: U.S. FERC backs jurisdiction split on Calif. power.

text.p: The U.S. Federal Energy Regulatory Commission Wednesday approved with minor changes a proposal by California's big electric utilities for splitting federal and state jurisdiction over their power lines.
The commission largely backed the utilities' view of which facilities were used for transmission, regulated by the FERC, and which were for local distribution, regulated by the state.

FERC commissioners repeatedly stressed that they had deferred to California's regulators' recommendations in drawing the lines between transmission and distribution facilities, avoiding a battle over state and federal control.
"This is evidence, not just a promise, that we will work with the states in a cooperative way," Commissioner William Massey said at the FERC meeting where the order was approved.
Wednesday's order was the FERC's first step toward sorting out federal jurisdiction issues over California's move to give all consumers freedom to choose their power suppliers.

The order was "critically important to ensure that state regulators retain the hook they need" to oversee local distribution rates and utilities' recovery of stranded costs as the market becomes competitive, said Commissioner Donald Santa.

California's three major utilities -- Pacific Gas and Electric Co, Edison International's Southern California Edison Co, and Enova Corp's San Diego Gas and Electric -- followed guidelines for characterizing transmission and distribution set out by the FERC last April.

In its Order 888, requiring all utilities to open their transmission lines to competing power producers, the FERC said it would view facilities as local distribution if, among other factors, they were close to retail customers, were mainly radial, and had reduced voltage.
For PG&E and SDG&E, the split between transmission and distribution facilities was generally at a lower voltage than for SoCal Edison's lines.
SoCal Edison viewed its lines between 60 kilovolts and 138 kilovolts mainly as local distribution, while the other two utilities treated those lines as transmission.
FERC reserved the right to review the jurisdictional split as the market evolved and use of the lines changed.

The commission has yet to rule on more difficult issues tied to California's market restructuring, including the setting up of an independent transmission system operator and a power exchange for selling electricity.
